pages.text: Maya loved playing soccer more than anything in the world. But sometimes, right in the middle of a big game, her chest would feel tight and her breathing would get hard. Maya had asthma — and that was okay, because she knew exactly what to do.
pages.imagePrompt: A cheerful girl with a soccer ball on a sunny green field, wearing a red jersey, warm watercolor illustration, child-friendly, no text

pages.text: One afternoon at practice, Maya had to stop running. Her chest felt squeezed, like something was pressing on it from the inside. She sat on the bench and wondered, 'Why does this keep happening to me?'
pages.imagePrompt: A girl sitting on a sports bench looking thoughtful and a little worried, holding her chest gently, soft watercolor illustration, child-friendly, no text

pages.text: Her doctor, Dr. Patel, sat with Maya after the game. 'Your lungs have tiny airways inside them,' she explained gently. 'With asthma, those airways sometimes get narrow. It is not your fault — your lungs just need a little extra help sometimes.'
pages.imagePrompt: A kind woman doctor sitting and talking warmly with a young girl in a bright clinic, watercolor illustration, gentle and reassuring, no text

pages.text: 'This inhaler is your best teammate,' said Dr. Patel, handing Maya the small blue device. 'When you feel that tightness, two puffs open your airways back up. Always keep it close to you — it is your superpower.'
pages.imagePrompt: A girl holding a small blue inhaler proudly, smiling with confidence, bright cheerful colors, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Maya took two puffs, waited, and felt her breathing open up like a window swinging wide. She jogged back onto the field, scored two goals, and high-fived her whole team.
pages.imagePrompt: A joyful girl scoring a soccer goal, arms raised in celebration, teammates cheering around her, sunny day, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Just like Maya, you have asthma — and just like Maya, you are brave and strong. Your inhaler is always on your side. Keep playing, keep running, and keep being amazing. You have got this.
pages.imagePrompt: A confident smiling girl holding an inhaler up like a trophy, rainbow in the background, warm glowing colors, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Jake loved drawing cartoons in his sketchbook every single day. But one Monday morning, Jake woke up feeling awful — his whole body ached, he felt very hot, and he was totally exhausted. Jake had the flu.
pages.imagePrompt: A boy lying in bed with a sketchbook nearby, looking tired and unwell, warm cozy bedroom, soft watercolor illustration, child-friendly, no text

pages.text: Jake's arms and legs felt heavy like wet sand. His head hurt, his throat was sore, and even lifting his pencil felt too hard. 'Will I feel like this forever?' he thought quietly.
pages.imagePrompt: A boy wrapped in a blanket on a couch, looking sad and tired, dim cozy lighting, soft gentle watercolor, no text

pages.text: Mom brought Jake to Dr. Kim, who listened to his chest. 'The flu is caused by a tiny germ called a virus,' Dr. Kim said kindly. 'Your body is working very hard right now to fight it — that is why you feel so tired and achy.'
pages.imagePrompt: A kind doctor with a stethoscope talking to a boy and his mom in a bright warm clinic, gentle smiling expression, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: 'The best thing you can do is rest and drink lots of water,' said Dr. Kim. 'Your body has special fighters called white blood cells, and sleep helps them win the battle. I will also give you medicine to help with the fever and the aches.'
pages.imagePrompt: A boy sleeping peacefully in bed with a glass of water on the nightstand, soft warm light, cozy watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: After five days of rest, soup, and his favourite cartoons on TV, Jake woke up and felt like himself again. He grabbed his sketchbook and drew a comic about a superhero who defeated the flu monster — starring himself.
pages.imagePrompt: A happy boy sitting up in bed drawing in a sketchbook, bright cheerful colors, sunlight coming through the window, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Getting the flu is no fun at all — but your body knows exactly how to fight back. Rest up, drink your water, and take your medicine. Just like Jake, you will be back to doing what you love very soon.
pages.imagePrompt: A healthy cheerful boy outside in fresh air with his sketchbook, bright sunny day, arms open wide, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Lily loved dancing. She practised her twirls and jumps every single day after school. But one evening, Lily felt very warm and shivery at the same time, and dancing was the last thing she wanted to do. She had a fever.
pages.imagePrompt: A girl in a dance outfit sitting on the floor looking unwell, warm cozy room, soft watercolor illustration, child-friendly, no text

pages.text: Lily's forehead felt hot when Grandma touched it. Her cheeks were red and her body felt wobbly and strange. She curled up on the couch and wondered why she felt so different.
pages.imagePrompt: A grandmother gently touching a girl's forehead as she lies on a couch wrapped in a blanket, warm loving scene, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Mom called the nurse, who explained in a calm, kind voice: 'A fever means your body's temperature has gone up on purpose. It is actually your body turning up the heat to kill the germs making you sick. Your body is fighting hard for you.'
pages.imagePrompt: A mom on the phone with a nurse, sitting next to her daughter on the couch, warm reassuring scene, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: 'Give her children's medicine to bring the temperature down so she feels comfortable,' said the nurse. 'Keep drinking cool water and rest under a light blanket. Her body is doing exactly what it should — let it do its job.'
pages.imagePrompt: A girl drinking a glass of cool water, mom nearby with medicine, soft warm home setting, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: By the next morning, Lily's fever was completely gone. She ate some toast, drank her orange juice, and by afternoon she was back at the dance studio, twirling like nothing had ever happened.
pages.imagePrompt: A girl twirling happily in a dance studio, bright colours, big smile, light and joyful, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: When you have a fever, remember — your body is not broken. It is working hard to protect you. Rest, drink water, take your medicine, and trust your amazing body. You will be back on your feet very soon.
pages.imagePrompt: A healthy girl with arms stretched wide in a sunny dance studio, rainbow light through a window, warm hopeful colors, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Carlos could build anything with LEGO — castles, spaceships, even a working crane. But this week, Carlos kept coughing and coughing, so much that it was hard to concentrate on anything at all.
pages.imagePrompt: A boy sitting at a table full of colourful LEGO bricks, coughing into his elbow, slightly frustrated look, warm watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Every few minutes — hack, hack, hack! Carlos coughed so much his throat felt scratchy and raw. He was worried. 'Is something really wrong with me?' he asked his mom.
pages.imagePrompt: A boy sitting on a couch with a worried expression, hand on his throat, mom sitting beside him looking reassuring, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: At the clinic, Dr. Osei listened to Carlos's chest. 'A cough is actually something very clever your body does,' she said. 'When something irritates your airways, your body coughs to push it out and clear the path. Your lungs are doing their job.'
pages.imagePrompt: A friendly woman doctor listening to a boy's chest with a stethoscope in a bright colourful clinic, warm and reassuring, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: 'Drink warm liquids like soup or honey water — they soothe your throat,' said Dr. Osei. 'Try sleeping with your head on an extra pillow to help the mucus drain. And give yourself time to rest. Your body is working hard.'
pages.imagePrompt: A boy drinking a warm mug of honey tea, cozy blanket, steam rising from the mug, soft warm lighting, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Carlos drank so much warm honey tea that his mom joked he was becoming a tea expert. Within a week, the cough had almost disappeared, and he finished building his biggest LEGO spaceship ever.
pages.imagePrompt: A happy healthy boy proudly holding a completed LEGO spaceship, big smile, bright cheerful colours, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Your cough is your body protecting your lungs — it is actually a superpower. Be patient with yourself, stay warm, and drink plenty of fluids. You will be back to building incredible things before you know it.
pages.imagePrompt: A confident boy standing tall next to his LEGO spaceship, bright sunny window behind him, warm hopeful colours, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Zoe loved springtime — the flowers, the warm sun, and playing in the park with her dog, Biscuit. But every spring, her eyes would get itchy and watery, and she would sneeze so many times she lost count. Zoe had seasonal allergies.
pages.imagePrompt: A girl playing in a park with a fluffy dog, flowers blooming around her, sneezing with a red runny nose, bright spring day, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: One afternoon in the park, Zoe's eyes turned red and puffy and her nose would not stop running. She felt miserable. 'Why does this always happen right when the weather gets nice?' she sighed.
pages.imagePrompt: A girl sitting on a park bench with puffy red eyes and a tissue, looking sad, flowers in the background, soft watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Dr. Nkosi explained it with a warm smile. 'You have allergies, which means your body's defence system gets a bit overexcited when it detects pollen — tiny dust from flowers and trees. Your body thinks it is dangerous and tries to flush it out. That is the sneezing and watery eyes.'
pages.imagePrompt: A friendly doctor showing a girl a diagram of a flower and tiny pollen dots, warm colourful clinic setting, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: 'We have two helpers for you,' said Dr. Nkosi. 'A daily allergy tablet will calm your body's reaction. And try wearing sunglasses outdoors to keep pollen away from your eyes. Wash your face and hands after playing outside too.'
pages.imagePrompt: A girl proudly wearing cool sunglasses outdoors and holding an allergy tablet, bright and cheerful, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: With her allergy tablet every morning and her cool new sunglasses, Zoe ran through the park with Biscuit all spring long. Her eyes still got a tiny bit itchy sometimes — but she did not let it slow her down at all.
pages.imagePrompt: A girl running joyfully in a park with sunglasses on and a dog running beside her, flowers everywhere, big smile, bright watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Allergies can be annoying, but they do not have to stop you from enjoying life. Your tablet, your sunglasses, and a quick face wash are all the tools you need. Get outside, play, and enjoy every single beautiful day.
pages.imagePrompt: A girl with sunglasses and arms wide open in a sunny park, dog jumping beside her, flowers and blue sky, warm hopeful watercolor, no text

pages.text: Ethan's tummy started hurting right after dinner. Before long, he felt a horrible wavy feeling in his stomach — and then he got sick and threw up. Ethan felt scared and a little embarrassed. But Mom was right there beside him.
pages.imagePrompt: A boy sitting on a bathroom floor looking pale and upset, mom crouching beside him with a gentle hand on his back, soft warm watercolor, no text

pages.text: Ethan lay back in bed feeling shaky and confused. 'Why did that happen?' he asked quietly. 'Am I going to keep being sick?' He pulled his blanket tighter and hoped someone could explain.
pages.imagePrompt: A pale boy lying in bed with a worried look, clutching his blanket, soft dim cozy bedroom, gentle watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Mom called the nurse, who spoke in a calm, kind voice. 'Vomiting happens when your stomach detects something wrong — like a tummy bug,' the nurse explained. 'Your stomach is actually protecting you by getting rid of whatever is bothering it. It is doing exactly the right thing.'
pages.imagePrompt: A mom sitting beside her son's bed on the phone, looking reassured, soft warm bedroom lighting, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: 'The most important thing now is tiny sips of water,' said the nurse. 'Not big gulps — just small sips every few minutes. Your tummy needs to rest before you can eat. A few crackers or plain toast later will help settle things down nicely.'
pages.imagePrompt: A boy taking a tiny careful sip of water from a glass, mom holding crackers nearby, soft cozy home setting, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Ethan rested, sipped his water slowly, and nibbled crackers throughout the day. By evening the awful feeling was completely gone. He woke up the next morning hungry for breakfast — and that felt like the best sign in the whole world.
pages.imagePrompt: A boy happily eating breakfast the next morning, sunny kitchen, big smile, orange juice on the table, bright cheerful watercolor, no text

pages.text: Throwing up is scary and yucky — but it means your body was protecting you. Small sips, rest, and patience are what you need. You will feel completely like yourself again soon, and your body will have done an amazing job.
pages.imagePrompt: A healthy cheerful boy standing outside with a big smile, fresh air and sunshine, warm hopeful colors, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Josh loved drawing superheroes in his cozy room more than anything. But today, his head started to ache with sharp pain waves, making it hard to focus on his art.
pages.imagePrompt: A boy sitting at a desk drawing superheroes, pressing his hand to his forehead in pain, cozy warm bedroom, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: His mom came in to help, gently placing a warm compress on his forehead while he rested in bed. She stayed by his side, making sure he felt safe and comfortable while his body worked on getting better.
pages.imagePrompt: A mom gently placing a warm compress on her son's forehead as he rests in bed, soft cozy bedroom, loving and warm, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Eating some warm soup and healthy food will help your body stay strong, his mom whispered as he took careful sips. He knew that fueling his body with good things was the best way to chase the headache away.
pages.imagePrompt: A boy sitting up in bed taking careful sips of warm soup, mom smiling beside him, cozy warm lighting, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: After a long, quiet rest, Josh woke up feeling amazing and full of energy again. He grabbed his crayons and finished his masterpiece, showing everyone that a little rest was all he needed to feel like a hero.
pages.imagePrompt: A boy sitting up bright and happy at his desk finishing a superhero drawing, big smile, sunny cozy room, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Sam loved music more than anything. He played piano, sang in the school choir, and always had a song stuck in his head. But one night, Sam woke up with a sharp throbbing pain deep inside his ear. He had an earache, and it hurt a lot.
pages.imagePrompt: A boy sitting up in bed at night holding his ear in pain, a small piano visible in the background, dim warm bedroom, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Sam held his ear with both hands. The pain was deep inside, like something was pressing hard from within. He could not sleep and he felt like he might cry. 'What is happening in there?' he thought.
pages.imagePrompt: A boy sitting on his bed holding both hands over his ear, looking distressed, soft nighttime bedroom lighting, gentle watercolor, no text

pages.text: In the morning, Mom took Sam to Dr. Reyes, who looked gently inside his ear with a small light. 'You have an ear infection,' Dr. Reyes said. 'Sometimes germs get into the space behind your eardrum and cause swelling and pressure — that deep pain you feel is from that pressure.'
pages.imagePrompt: A kind doctor gently looking into a boy's ear with a small otoscope light, mom watching from beside him, warm clinic setting, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: 'I am giving you antibiotic medicine to fight the germs,' said Dr. Reyes. 'A warm cloth held gently against your ear can also help soothe the pain. Take every single dose of your medicine, even when you start feeling better — that is really important.'
pages.imagePrompt: A boy holding a warm cloth against his ear, medicine bottle on the table, mom nearby, cozy home setting, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Sam took his medicine every day exactly as Dr. Reyes said. Within two days the pain started fading. By the end of the week, he was back at the piano playing his favourite song with both hands — louder and happier than ever.
pages.imagePrompt: A happy healthy boy playing piano with a big joyful smile, bright colourful music room, sunlight streaming in, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: An earache is painful, but your medicine is working hard for you. Take every single dose, keep your ear warm and dry, and rest. Your ears will be back to hearing all the beautiful music in the world very soon.
pages.imagePrompt: A boy standing by his piano with arms out and a huge smile, musical notes floating around him, warm bright colors, hopeful watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Alex was eleven and had started noticing something new — small red bumps appearing on her forehead and cheeks. Some kids at school had them too. Alex felt a little self-conscious and wondered what was happening to her skin.
pages.imagePrompt: A preteen girl looking in a bathroom mirror touching her cheek gently with a curious expression, soft warm bathroom lighting, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Alex looked in the mirror and felt frustrated. The bumps were hard to ignore. She tried squeezing one and it only got worse. 'Why is this happening to me?' she thought. 'Did I do something wrong?'
pages.imagePrompt: A girl with a frustrated expression looking closely at her reflection in a mirror, soft watercolor, warm lighting, no text

pages.text: Mom took Alex to see Dr. Chen, who spoke to her like an equal. 'What you have is called acne, and it is extremely common at your age,' said Dr. Chen. 'Your body is changing, and your skin is producing more oil than usual. That oil can block tiny pores and create those bumps. It has nothing to do with being dirty or doing something wrong.'
pages.imagePrompt: A friendly woman doctor talking earnestly with a preteen girl, reassuring and open body language, bright modern clinic, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: 'Here is your simple skincare routine,' said Dr. Chen. 'Wash your face gently twice a day — morning and night — with a mild cleanser. Do not scrub hard and do not squeeze pimples, because that makes them worse. I will also give you a gentle cream to apply at night that helps clear blocked pores.'
pages.imagePrompt: A girl washing her face gently at a bathroom sink, face cleanser and small cream tube on the counter, soft warm bathroom, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Alex started her new morning and night routine without skipping a single day. It took a few weeks, but slowly her skin started to clear. She stopped worrying every time she passed a mirror and focused on the things that made her feel like herself.
pages.imagePrompt: A confident preteen girl smiling at herself in the mirror, looking happy and comfortable, bright cheerful bathroom, watercolor illustration, no text

pages.text: Acne is one of the most normal things a growing body does. It does not define how you look or who you are. Take care of your skin gently, be patient with yourself, and know that this is just one small part of a big, amazing journey of growing up.
pages.imagePrompt: A confident smiling girl standing tall in natural light, happy and at ease, warm glowing colours, hopeful watercolor illustration, no text
